analysis.one_liner: Cuts the corporate tax rate from 35% to 23% and exempts foreign subsidiary dividends from U.S. tax.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut the corporate tax rate by more than a third and permanently shield foreign profits died without a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 23% and made permanent a deduction that lets U.S. companies bring home dividends from their overseas subsidiaries without paying the normal U.S. tax on those profits. Sponsor Rep. Tim Scott (R-SC) and 63 Republican cosponsors supported it. It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee in March 2011 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporate shareholders and large companies — especially multinationals with controlled foreign corporations — would gain a lower tax bill on both domestic and foreign-source income. A 12-point corporate rate cut plus a permanent exemption of repatriated dividends would sharply reduce federal revenue, the burden of which falls on other taxpayers or future borrowing.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 23% and flattens the graduated corporate rate structure to a flat 23%, cutting tax bills for all profitable corporations [S2][S3].

Repeals the limits on the dividends received deduction for dividends a U.S. company receives from its controlled foreign corporations and makes the deduction permanent, moving toward a territorial system in which foreign profits are largely untaxed by the United States [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, bears the revenue loss. Because corporate taxes are partly borne by capital owners and partly offset by either deficits or other taxes, the cost is spread across the public while the benefit is concentrated among shareholders.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top corporate rate by 12 percentage points and permanently exempting repatriated foreign dividends would substantially reduce federal revenue, requiring larger deficits or offsetting tax increases elsewhere [S2][S3].

A permanent dividends-received deduction for controlled foreign corporations would encourage companies to book income in low-tax foreign jurisdictions, since profits shifted overseas would flow back to U.S. owners largely tax-free [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow narrowly to corporate shareholders, while the cost — a large, permanent revenue loss that makes borrowing or other taxes higher — is spread across everyone. The bill contained no revenue offsets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in March 2011, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Scott introduced the bill on March 4, 2011 and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day [S1][S5].
The Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, and it received no further floor action for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No corporation gained, since the tax cuts never took effect; the outcome preserved the existing corporate rate and the taxation of repatriated foreign dividends, sparing the Treasury the revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, which kept current corporate tax law

for.name: Rep. Tim Scott
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the corporate rate to 23% and make the foreign dividends deduction permanent.

sides.party_line_note: All 63 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never reached a vote, so no one's floor position is recorded.

industries.note: A 23% top rate plus a permanent deduction for dividends from controlled foreign corporations would cut their tax bills sharply, particularly for companies with extensive overseas operations. The revenue loss would be borne by the broader taxpayer base.

Lower corporate taxes flow to shareholders through higher after-tax returns; but most public-market shares are held broadly, including by retirement savers, so benefits are spread unevenly and skew toward wealthier households.
The bill had no revenue offsets; the combined rate cut and permanent foreign-dividend exemption would have raised deficits or forced other tax increases.
